stem:
You are to plan an experiment to compare the rates of hydrolysis of 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane.

When a halogenoalkane is warmed with aqueous silver nitrate dissolved in ethanol, water slowly hydrolyses it: $\ce{C4H9X + H2O -> C4H9OH + H+ + X-}$. The halide ions released form a precipitate with silver ions, $\ce{Ag+(aq) + X-(aq) -> AgX(s)}$. The time taken for a precipitate to first appear can be used as a measure of the rate: relative rate ∝ 1/time.

Data: density of 1-bromobutane 1.27 g cm⁻³; Ar: H 1.0, C 12.0, Br 79.9. Halogenoalkanes are flammable and harmful; silver nitrate stains skin and is corrosive to eyes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Predict the order of the rates of hydrolysis, explain your prediction, and describe in words a suitable chart or graph of the expected results.

points.description: Prediction: 1-iodobutane fastest, then 1-bromobutane, then 1-chlorobutane slowest, because C–I is the weakest C–X bond and C–Cl the strongest (bond strength, not polarity, decides)
A bar chart of relative rate (1/time) for each halogenoalkane, or a plot of 1/time against C–X bond energy falling as bond energy increases

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rate order: iodo > bromo > chloro, because the C–X bond energy decreases from C–Cl to C–I, so the C–I bond breaks most easily. Results can be shown as a bar chart with the three halogenoalkanes on the x-axis and 1/time (relative rate) on the y-axis; the iodo bar is tallest and the chloro bar shortest (or 1/time falls as the C–X bond energy increases).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Identify the independent and dependent variables, and two variables that must be controlled.

points.description: Independent: the halogen in the halogenoalkane (type of C–X bond); dependent: time for the precipitate to appear
Controlled (any two): temperature; amount (mol) of halogenoalkane; volume and concentration of silver nitrate; volume of ethanol; size of test tubes

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Independent variable: the halogen (Cl, Br or I). Dependent variable: the time for a precipitate to first appear. Controlled variables: the temperature of the water bath and the amount of each halogenoalkane (also the volume and concentration of silver nitrate and the volume of ethanol).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Equal amounts, 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol, of each halogenoalkane are to be used. Calculate the volume of 1-bromobutane needed, in cm³, to three significant figures.
parts.explanation: Mass = 1.00 × 10⁻³ × 136.9 = 0.137 g; volume = 0.137 ÷ 1.27 = 0.108 cm³ (measured with a graduated pipette or about two drops). Giving the mass in grams instead of the volume is a common slip.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Mass = 1.00 × 10⁻³ × 136.9 = 0.137 g; volume = 0.137 ÷ 1.27 = 0.108 cm³ (measured with a graduated pipette or about two drops). Giving the mass in grams instead of the volume is a common slip.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe a step-by-step method, naming the apparatus.

points.description: Put the same volume of ethanol (e.g. 1.0 cm³) into each of three test tubes and add the calculated, equal amount of each halogenoalkane using a graduated pipette; label the tubes
Place these tubes and a tube of aqueous silver nitrate (e.g. 0.05 mol dm⁻³) in a thermostatted water bath at about 50 °C until they reach the bath temperature (check with a thermometer)
Add the same volume of silver nitrate (e.g. 1.0 cm³) to each tube, mix, and start a stopwatch at the moment of addition
Record the time when a precipitate first appears (view against a black background); repeat the whole experiment and take mean times

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Measure 1.0 cm³ of ethanol into each of three labelled test tubes and add the calculated volume of each halogenoalkane from a graduated pipette. Stand the tubes, and a fourth tube containing 0.05 mol dm⁻³ aqueous silver nitrate, in a water bath at 50 °C until they reach that temperature. Add 1.0 cm³ of the silver nitrate to each halogenoalkane tube, mixing, and start a stopwatch. Watch each tube against a dark background and record the time at which a precipitate first appears. Repeat the experiment twice more and calculate mean times.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State one safety precaution, linked to a hazard.

points.description: e.g. no naked flames (heat with a water bath) because ethanol and halogenoalkanes are flammable; or gloves and eye protection because silver nitrate is corrosive and stains skin

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Use an electrically heated water bath, not a Bunsen burner, because ethanol and the halogenoalkanes are flammable.

points.description: Columns: halogenoalkane; time for precipitate / s for each repeat; mean time / s; relative rate (1/mean time) / s⁻¹, with units in the headings

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Columns headed: halogenoalkane | time 1 / s | time 2 / s | time 3 / s | mean time / s | relative rate (1/t) / s⁻¹.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: In a trial, the precipitate appeared after 48 s with 1-iodobutane and after 1250 s with 1-chlorobutane. Calculate how many times faster the hydrolysis of 1-iodobutane is, to two significant figures.
parts.explanation: Relative rate ∝ 1/t, so the ratio = (1/48) ÷ (1/1250) = 1250 ÷ 48 = 26 times faster.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Relative rate ∝ 1/t, so the ratio = (1/48) ÷ (1/1250) = 1250 ÷ 48 = 26 times faster.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Explain why ethanol is used in the mixture.

points.description: Halogenoalkanes do not mix with water; ethanol dissolves both the halogenoalkane and the aqueous silver nitrate, so they form one phase and can react

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The halogenoalkanes are insoluble in water, but ethanol mixes with both the halogenoalkane and the aqueous silver nitrate, giving a single solution in which hydrolysis can occur.

explanation: Predicted order I > Br > Cl (C–X bond strength); 0.108 cm³ of 1-bromobutane; iodo about 26 times faster than chloro in the trial.
hints: Mass = moles × Mr; volume = mass ÷ density.
